title: The learned man of Benares
hookLine: tradition says a Benares pandit tested Nanak with learning and heard him sing the Oankar

cards: A child at a kitchen table, tracing the alphabet with a fat pencil. A says apple. B says ball.
Every letter is a door to one small thing. Somewhere along the way, the letters stop being seen at all; they become the furniture of reading.

Today's sakhi takes us to Benares, a city of scholars on the river Ganges, where a learned man meets a traveler and they end up talking about letters, of all things. Not apple and ball. Something much bigger.

teach.b: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana arrive in Benares and sit by the river. A pandit, a learned man of the city, notices this traveler with no sacred marks, no scholar's books, and a musician at his side.
Some tellings give him a name, Chatur Das. He comes to test the Guru. What have you studied?
Tradition says Nanak answered by singing, and the hymn he sang was the Oankar, a long composition now in the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the clever thing about it.
A pandit taught with letters: students wrote them on a wooden slate, one by one. The Oankar takes the pandit's own tools and turns them.

teach.h: EACH LETTER A DOOR TO THE ONE.
teach.b: Its verses move through the letters, and each letter becomes a door to the One. It opens with Oankar itself, the One, from whom even Brahma, the creator god of the pandit's own books, came into being.
Then, letter by letter, it speaks of God, of the mind, of the false and the true, of what learning is for. So the Guru doesn't throw learning away.
He takes the alphabet a scholar loves and shows him where every letter points. In the tellings, the pandit listens, and bows.
Notice who bows: not a fool, but a learned man. And not because he lost an argument, but because he heard his own learning sung back to him, deeper than he'd been reading it.
Sikh tradition honors study; the Gurus wrote, collected and taught.
Learning bows, in this story, when it remembers what it's about.

how: The Oankar, which tradition links to Guru Nanak's meeting with a pandit, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is sung and studied by Sikhs, verse by verse through the letters.

games.q: you're a learned man of Benares. a traveler with no books and a musician at his side sits by your river. what do you do?
o: go and test him with learning.
ask him to leave the city.
games.why: tradition says the pandit tested Nanak, and the Guru answered by singing the Oankar. the learned man listened, and bowed.

practice: Pick a letter, any letter in any alphabet you know, and say its sound quietly. Let it lead you to one word that matters to you, a name, a place, a quality you want more of, and hold that word for the rest of the sit.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and notice the letters in it.
